Nonlocal gravity models serve as effective descriptions for the gravitational dynamics of neutron star interiors. Extra-large scale massive multiple-input multiple-output (XL-MIMO) systems represent a promising solution for delivering ultra-high data rates in environments with high user density. Because the physical dimensions of XL-MIMO arrays are comparable to the distances separating user groups, significant spatial loss occurs between remote groups and the array, resulting in non-negligible interference between groups. Additionally, the random nature of user locations within a group, combined with limited detection range, means that not all users can be seen by the array at any given time. This paper introduces a new time-division multiple-access (TDMA) protocol called Non-Intersecting Visibility Regions (NIVR)-based Random Access (RA), which exploits the fact that simultaneous access by intersecting visibility regions (IVR)-based users causes strong interference. The protocol operates in two phases: first, IVR-based users transmit their associations, and second, NIVR-based users perform random access. Under ideal channel estimation conditions, a new protocol optimizing time allocation for the NIVR-based random access phase is proposed. Simulation results demonstrate that the NIVR-based RA protocol yields higher sum rates than conventional RA methods. Furthermore, when channel estimation errors are considered, the sum rates of conventional protocols decline significantly, whereas the NIVR-based RA protocol maintains superior performance. These findings confirm that XL-MIMO systems can effectively support random access for groups of cells, with the NIVR-based approach offering the most effective solution. The practical feasibility of this protocol is further validated by a real-world simulation involving a building with 110 access points and 75 stations. Building on this feasibility, the paper concludes by formulating an optimization problem aimed at determining the optimal number of XL-MIMO arrays required to serve a specific area via NIVR-based random access.

Although neural language models have largely replaced traditional $N$-gram models due to superior performance, our findings suggest that $N$-grams still offer advantages in specific scenarios, such as improving sampling-based generation quality and accelerating inference speed for certain tasks. Statistical hypothesis testing plays a crucial role in identifying non-random patterns within data to uncover hidden behaviors, making it especially critical for auditing algorithms used in high-stakes domains like hiring, lending, and hiring. While modern applications increasingly rely on powerful deep learning-based testing frameworks, these approaches often lack sufficient statistical precision to detect subtle, discriminatory behaviors. In contrast, permutation testing offers an exact, distribution-free method for significance level control. However, existing implementations of this test are approximately precise, failing to meet the precision required for effective data-driven behavior detection. This paper introduces a new algorithm that achieves exact 2-p precision and can be further customized for t-precision. The algorithm operates in O (n log²(n)/2) complexity to reach 2-p precision. For achieving t-precision (where t > 2), the complexity becomes O (n log^(t+1)(n)). Demonstrating the value of this increased precision, we apply the exact 2-p test to detect specific unfair behaviors in CV selection and rejection algorithms. Our findings reveal that state-of-the-art algorithms require a sample size approximately 100,000 times larger than what was used in prior experiments to achieve a 5% significance level, whereas our method can exactely test significance levels as low as 0.99%. Applications of this exact testing approach are essential for comprehensively evaluating algorithmic fairness assumptions. Additionally, this work provides a rigorous statistical framework for assessing the discriminatory behavior of "black-box" algorithms without relying on engaging them. The proposed framework also serves as a practical tool for compliance with anti-discrimination regulations, which often mandate the ability to detect rather than merely prevent discriminatory outcomes. Implementing this framework within the context of the US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission's formal legal standard for discrimination detection is also discussed. Code availability is confirmed for the exact 2-p testing approach as well as a near-exact 3-p version.

We implemented a novel approach to simulate the ground state wavefunction of a quantum harmonic oscillator subjected to uniform acceleration or subjected to time-dependent driving forces, via projection Monte Carlo techniques. Employing path integral formalism, the ground state wavefunction was estimated through Monte Carlo integration over both the initial wavefunction and imaginary time evolution operators. These components were realized using specific parametric ansatzes and Metropolis updates within a Metropolis-Hastings algorithm. Leveraging Neuman-Euler expansion, we simulated an accelerated oscillator with an mass of 100 tons under a vertical force of 10 N, achieving a simulation accuracy of $10^{-2}$ with 10,000 samples. Furthermore, we investigated the system under time-dependent driving forces, successfully reproducing an expected sinusoidal behavior. Notably, this work represents the first application of projection Monte Carlo methods to simple quantum systems to solve for their wavefunctions under external driving forces. While directly applicable to the harmonic oscillator, the framework can potentially be extended to more complex systems, such as many-body systems, to address problems currently solved by variational Monte Carlo methods. Distinct from standard Metropolis sampling of configurations, our approach samples paths; consequently, it aligns closely with path integral Monte Carlo (PIMC) and discrete time Monte Carlo (DisTiMC) techniques used for computing partition functions. However, our method specifically targets the ground state wavefunction. Validation against analytical solutions confirmed the effectiveness of this projection Monte Carlo approach for simulating simple driven quantum systems. Horn clauses serve as a powerful framework for integrating semantic information into logical reasoning about programs, enabling the derivation of correctness properties through proof procedures. In the context of classical Hoare reasoning, recent advancements have introduced expectations—numeric assertions—to replace boolean ones, facilitating quantitative correctness analyses via probabilistic reasoning. This approach allows for error-free execution and undecidables property proofs. Furthermore, recent work demonstrated that expectation reasoning can be made constructive with a constructive variant of the Herbrand-Engeler theorem, yielding a probabilistic version of Hoare reasoning capable of establishing error probabilities for specific executions. While this constructive reasoning has been demonstrated for recent probabilistic imperative languages like MTL and GCE, such frameworks remain novel. In this article, we present a constructive relational Hoare reasoning system for expectations applicable to a recent quantum language incorporating side effects and probabilistic choices. We validate the soundness of this system within a quantum meta-calculus and illustrate its utility with multiple examples. Additionally, we sketch potential directions for extending this approach to quantum software engineering, including error probability analysis, refinement, and contracts. Although our meta-calculus incorporates gradual typing and relies on recent theories of relational reasoning for both classical and quantum Hoare triples, our proof utilizes standard induction and congruence arguments specific to the quantum meta-calculus, distinguishing it from proof methods used in gradual reasoning for classical or gradual type theory. Notably, our system employs the Jordaens meta-calculus for quantum relational reasoning, which supports reasoning about error probabilities in quantum programs, a capability absent in recent Meta-Calcules for error reasoning in classical programs. We conclude by outlining potential research directions. The source code for this project is accessible at https://github.com/abdulrahman-alkhatib/QRHE.

This study addresses the under sampled noise bias when applying Maximum Entropy Method (MEM) reconstruction to vector magnetic field data from the VIP* instrument on the French VTT telescope. It is important to note that further development and detailed design work are required before such a system could be deployed on space-based platforms.

We introduce a fully relativistic, first-principles theoretical framework designed to calculate the spectral properties of magnetic impurities situated on superconducting surfaces, specifically targeting the spin-dependent local states. Focusing on the Yurta--Rusinov (YSR) state, we formulate a self-consistent approach to derive its wave function and energy. Within this model, the local coherency amplitude and binding energy of the YSR state are determined as functions of the local density of states (LDOS) on the impurity site, enabling the extraction of the order parameter at that specific location. Consequently, this method facilitates an explicit investigation into how the binding energy of the YSR state correlates with the spectral gap narrowing of the underlying surface. To validate this formalism, we analyze the electronic states of an Mn adatom and various Mn clusters ($N$=dimers to $N$=pentamers) on the Nb(110) surface. The calculated results for the Mn adatom align closely with recent experimental data, while the configurations of the Mn clusters on Nb(110) offer a theoretical foundation for guiding future experimental investigations. Ultimately, this study provides a theoretical examination of how electronic structure, magnetism, and superconductivity interact within these systems. These findings also demonstrate that the self-consistent Yurta--Rusinov state model effectively highlights the local character of the order parameter. The developed framework is universally applicable to exploring the spectral properties of local states in hybrid systems involving magnetic impurities on superconducting surfaces, such as investigating the physical origins of excited Yurta--Rusinov states in Fe adatoms on Nb(110) or the impact of different co-existing spin states in Mn clusters on Nb(110). Specifically, the approach can be utilized to assess the stability of individual yurta--Rusinov state configurations for various impurities on superconducting surfaces or to explore the influence of atomic site geometry, atomic environment, and material composition on the electronic states of local excitations in these materials. This research presents a framework for classifying the BST32,000 dataset, which contains 109,039 images and includes outlier samples. Although numerous studies have attempted to diagnose skin cancer using this dataset with varying strategies, it remains challenging due to the presence of outliers and a significant class imbalance. Prior works have attempted to address these issues through data selection, augmentation, and convolutional neural networks (CNNs). However, selecting the appropriate subset of data to optimize classification remains difficult. Leveraging the fact that outliers tend to cluster together, we propose an approach that identifies and removes these anomalous samples via entropy calculation before applying a CNN for the remaining tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that this method outperforms existing approaches on the BST32,000 dataset, achieving an AUC score of 0.9961, an F1 score of 0.8863, and a Macc value of 0.8514. To our knowledge, these metrics represent the highest performance recorded for this dataset. Furthermore, the classification decisions generated by our model provide a detailed breakdown of the data, highlighting the specific samples that were excluded from the final analysis. The source code for this project is accessible at: https://github.com/Abdul-As-salam/SkinCancer. We conclude by discussing further potential applications of this work. Keywords: Skin cancer, outlier samples, skin lesions, entropy, and BST32,000 dataset.

This work introduces an efficient Regime-Transition VBR (R-VBR) scheme specifically for muon-muon ($\mu^+\mu^-$) elastic and near-elastic scattering. Building upon a formal derivation of Regime-Transition VBR applicable to any high-energy particle scattering process, the study demonstrates that the R-VBR method yields superior efficiency compared to exact calculation techniques when handling elastic and forward-angle $\mu^+\mu^-$ scattering. A comparative evaluation of various one-loop electroweak correction methods reveals that for near-elastic $\mu^+\mu^-$ scattering, the R-VBR (specifically Vertex+Box) and Phase-Space (PS) approaches deliver consistent results with high efficiency. Furthermore, for center-of-mass energies exceeding a few TeV, this optimized R-VBR framework enables feasible one-loop electroweak correction calculations for a wide range of near-elastic processes. As a proof of concept, the report provides detailed computations for several representative near-elastic processes to validate the feasibility of this approach. Leveraging the new $\mu^+\mu^-$ collider concept, this method will support precise measurements of electroweak parameters and serve as a necessary foundation for physics projections at multi-loop levels and for defining observables suitable for muon-muon scattering experiments. The presented framework has been implemented in the \texttt{Muneloop} generator, which complements existing "munu" event generators by covering one-loop electroweak, pure QCD, and mixed one-loop corrections. Invariant manifolds, including fixed points and invariant lines or curves, play a crucial role in the stability analysis of high-dimensional dynamical systems. This communication introduces a general method for determining the existence of invariant surfaces within a specific class of fractional-order systems known as "additive" systems. The proposed approach relies on extending Pelletier's theorem, which was originally developed for second-order polynomial systems. Following the establishment of this general method, we demonstrate its application by deriving the conditions required for invariant surfaces in a concrete three-variable fractional-order system. Subsequently, these conditions are utilized to prove the non-existence of such surfaces in a specific numerical instance of this system. Finally, the significance of this finding is highlighted by adapting the Poincaré-Bendixson theory to a particular three-variable additive fractional-order system to derive a persistence of biodiversity result. To enable this adaptation, the general method for deriving invariant surface conditions is combined with the principle of invariance under coordinate transformations. Ultimately, this framework yields a generalized Perron-Brouwer theorem suitable for additive fractional-order systems. This work constitutes the first derivation of a Brunovský-like theorem for such systems, a result that supports the development of a general Poincaré invariance of dimension theory specifically tailored for fractional-order systems. Practical implementations of this Poincaré invariance principle are outlined to finalize the adaptation of the Poincaré-Bendixson theory for three-variable additive fractional-order systems. Supporting materials provide a rigorous mathematical formulation of the general method for determining invariant surface conditions and a detailed proof of the Poincaré invariance of dimension principle for these systems. Additive three-variable fractional-order systems serve as an ideal testbed for this methodology, as they function as the highest-dimensional linear fractional-order systems amenable to closed-loop control without exhibiting resonant phenomena associated with higher dimensions. The concept of the-cap ($\ast$) is defined as $\nu / \pi$ times the usual angle, where $\nu$ represents the Caputo fractional derivative order of the system.

This study addresses the inverse problem of a structural acoustic interaction using carbon fiber composite plates. The method involves creating a finite element model through shape optimization, where the boundary shape of a plate with known material properties is optimized to match an experimentally observed boundary deformation. The resulting inverted model is then validated against a previously unpublished model inverted by the same author. Experimental setups involve deforming the plates via a boundary actuator and generating internal vibrations using a shaker, with a laser vibrometer measuring the resulting deformation. The inverted model successfully predicted the deformation in the region excited by the shaker, confirming the approach's effectiveness. Additionally, the results indicate that adding boundary conditions to the inverted model's boundaries could further enhance prediction accuracy. Finally, this work presents a "proof of concept" rather than an optimal solution; future research should focus on refining the model and conducting more comprehensive validations. (C) 2020 Author(s). We introduce the simplest variant of scoto-seesaw Model B, a theory characterized by its minimal particle content required to generate neutrino mass via the seesaw mechanism, achieve a stable vacuum, and account for the correct neutrino mixing angles and mass scales. This extension of the Standard Model (SM) incorporates only three new fields: a singlet scalar, a heavy neutral neutrino, and a scalar mediator. We detail the model's parameter space and perform a comprehensive phenomenological analysis. Firstly, we map out the regions responsible for neutrino physics, metabolic stability, and dark matter (DM) viability. Secondly, focusing on the dark sector, we conduct an in-depth examination of the DM phenomenology within the viable parameter space. Our results demonstrate that, aside from specific intersections between neutrino and stability constraints, the co-annihilation and portal processes are sufficient to satisfy thermal DM requirements. Our findings further indicate that the simplest singlet scalar DM within this model is a "just right" cold DM candidate, exhibiting a mass of approximately 100 GeV, which aligns with current direct detection limits. Although these constraints are less stringent for a \textit{lightest} singlet scalar in generic scoto-seesaw models, our analysis shows that incorporating a second singlet scalar significantly enhances dark sector phenomenology by opens up additional co-annihilation and resonance annihilation channels. Finally, we investigate the simplicity of this model, its potential utility as an effective field theory beyond the scale of neutrino mass generation, and its fit within the landscape of Minimal Finite Field theories. While our findings confirm that the three-field scoto-seesaw Model B represents the simplest configuration capable of meeting all physical constraints, achieving further simplification would necessitate relaxing one of the following objectives: ensuring neutrino masses fall within observed limits, achieving dark matter abundance consistency with direct detection limits, or maintaining vacuum stability. This relationship ensures that a stable theory with dark matter abundance matching observational limits must possess at least one mass scale exceeding 100 GeV.
